title: Load Balancer: L4 vs L7
subtitle: Transport-layer packet forwarding vs Application-layer HTTP inspection, routing algorithms, health checks, and HA load balancer pairs.
keyTakeaways: Layer 4 (Transport) Load Balancers route based solely on IP + TCP/UDP port without decrypting payloads, achieving millions of packets/sec with sub-millisecond latency.
Layer 7 (Application) Load Balancers terminate TLS, parse HTTP headers/URLs/cookies, and perform content-based routing, rate limiting, and WAF inspection.
In production, high-scale architectures stack both: an Anycast/L4 tier (AWS NLB / IPVS) in front of a horizontally scaled fleet of L7 proxies (Envoy / NGINX / ALB).

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: A Load Balancer distributes incoming network traffic across a group of backend servers to maximize utilization and ensure no single node is overwhelmed. **Layer 4 (L4)** load balancers operate at the OSI Transport Layer (TCP/UDP): they inspect only the 5-tuple (Source IP, Source Port, Dest IP, Dest Port, Protocol), rewrite the destination IP/MAC via NAT (or Direct Server Return), and forward packets along the same TCP connection between client and server. **Layer 7 (L7)** load balancers act as full reverse proxies: they terminate the client's TCP and TLS connection, decrypt and parse the HTTP request, and open a separate pooled backend TCP connection based on URL path (`/v1/orders`), `Host` header, JWT claims, or cookies.
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: Layer 4 (Transport) Load Balancers route based solely on IP + TCP/UDP port without decrypting payloads, achieving millions of packets/sec with sub-millisecond latency.
**Problem Space & Invariants**: Layer 7 (Application) Load Balancers terminate TLS, parse HTTP headers/URLs/cookies, and perform content-based routing, rate limiting, and WAF inspection.
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: Distributed architectures apply specific implementation patterns and topologies for Load Balancer: L4 vs L7:
bullets: **Layer 4 Load Balancer (TCP / UDP Packet Level)**: Provides millions of qps per node, ultra-low latency (<100 microseconds), protocol-agnostic (works for raw tcp databases, mqtt, udp gaming, dns). Best suited for Edge ingress in front of L7 proxies, non-HTTP TCP/UDP protocols, and ultra-high-throughput media streaming (with DSR).

**Layer 7 Load Balancer (HTTP / gRPC Application Level)**: Provides smart routing by url/header/cookie, centralized tls termination, connection multiplexing, canary weight splitting, built-in waf and rate limiting. Best suited for Microservice API routing, gRPC load balancing (requires L7 to inspect HTTP/2 frames!), and canary deployments.
L4 Examples: AWS Network Load Balancer (NLB), Linux IPVS, Google Maglev, HAProxy (TCP mode).
L7 Examples: AWS Application Load Balancer (ALB), Envoy Proxy, NGINX, Cloudflare Edge.
Round Robin / Weighted Round Robin: Cycles sequentially; ideal when all requests have identical CPU cost.
Least Connections / Least Response Time (P2C): Essential for long-lived connections (WebSockets) or variable-latency queries (LLM inference, complex searches).

sections.heading: 3. Production Strengths: Where & How to Apply
sections.body: Production deployments apply Load Balancer: L4 vs L7 across targeted operational scenarios:
bullets: **Where to Use: High-Impact Scenarios**: Optimal for Edge ingress in front of L7 proxies, non-HTTP TCP/UDP protocols, and ultra-high-throughput media streaming (with DSR), suited for environments requiring Millions of QPS per node, ultra-low latency (<100 microseconds), protocol-agnostic (works for raw TCP databases, MQTT, UDP gaming, DNS).

**Where to Use: High-Throughput Scenarios**: Recommended for Microservice API routing, gRPC load balancing (requires L7 to inspect HTTP/2 frames!), and canary deployments, where Smart routing by URL/header/cookie, centralized TLS termination, connection multiplexing, canary weight splitting, built-in WAF and rate limiting.

**How to Use: Engineering Implementation**: Choosing how a load balancer picks a target node depends on whether requests have uniform cost or variable cost, and whether backend nodes cache data locally. Always establish explicit thresholds, measurement baselines, and automated monitoring.
**Architectural Leverage**: Provides predictable resource boundaries, bounds blast radius, and optimizes cost per transaction.

sections.heading: 4. Failure Modes & Trade-Offs: When to Avoid
sections.body: Improper implementation of Load Balancer: L4 vs L7 introduces operational bottlenecks and failure modes:
bullets: **Where to Avoid: Trade-Off Bottlenecks**: Avoid when constraints cannot tolerate: blind to http paths, headers, and cookies; cannot terminate tls (unless tls offload enabled), cannot do path-based microservice routing or waf.

**Where to Avoid: Complexity Ceiling**: Avoid when operational requirements do not justify: higher cpu and memory footprint (buffers payloads and maintains two tcp sockets), slightly higher latency (~1-2ms).
**Catastrophic Failure Modes**: Uncalibrated parameters can trigger queue exhaustion, thread starvation, cascading retry storms, and tail latency amplification.
**Operational Overhead**: Requires continuous observability (p95/p99 latency tracking, saturation alerts, and distributed tracing across hop boundaries).

sections.heading: 5. Staff+ Engineering Verdict & Interview Playbook
sections.body: Technical guidelines and evaluation criteria for Load Balancer: L4 vs L7:
bullets: **Staff+ Golden Rule**: In production, high-scale architectures stack both: an Anycast/L4 tier (AWS NLB / IPVS) in front of a horizontally scaled fleet of L7 proxies (Envoy / NGINX / ALB).

**Staff+ Interview Playbook**: Remember this critical nuance: **An L4 Load Balancer cannot properly load-balance gRPC or HTTP/2!** Because HTTP/2 multiplexes all requests over a single persistent TCP connection, an L4 LB will pin 100% of a caller's traffic to a single backend pod. You MUST use an L7 Load Balancer (like Envoy) to balance individual HTTP/2 streams.
